item.title: CFM Week 26 — 2 Samuel 11–12; 1 Kings 3; 6–9; 11: Hear Thou in Heaven Their Prayer
item.description: A 3h56m doctrinal deep dive on 2 Samuel 11–12 and 1 Kings 3; 6–9; 11 — a sustained meditation on one question: is my heart whole with God? Solomon charged Israel, "Let your heart therefore be perfect [Hebrew shalem — whole, undivided] with the Lord our God" (1 Kings 8:61), and the week is the cost of keeping that heart whole and the cost of letting it divide. Five movements. The first is David's fall (2 Samuel 11): not a single instant but a chain — a war sat out, a rooftop, a lingering look, a taking, and an escalating cover-up that ends in the murder of Uriah the Hittite, the loyal foreigner who keeps the covenant the king betrays. The second is Nathan, repentance, and the cost (2 Samuel 12; Psalm 51): the prophet's parable of the poor man's ewe lamb, "Thou art the man," David's total confession "I have sinned against the Lord," and the sober truth that the sin is put away yet the sword would not depart from his house. The third is Solomon's wisdom (1 Kings 3): asked "Ask what I shall give thee," the young king confesses "I am but a little child" and requests "an understanding heart" (Hebrew lev shomea, a hearing heart) — what we ask reveals what we treasure — even as a marriage of alliance with Egypt quietly plants the seed of his undoing. The fourth is the spine of the week, building and dedicating the temple (1 Kings 6–8; 9:1–9): stones set so silently "there was neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron heard in the house," cherubim and palm trees carving Eden in stone and gold, the cloud of glory filling the house, and Solomon kneeling with open hands in the longest prayer in the Old Testament — "the heaven of heavens cannot contain thee," and yet "hear thou in heaven… and when thou hearest, forgive" — the appointed meeting place where a sinful people is reconciled to a holy God, accepted by the Lord: "Mine eyes and mine heart shall be there perpetually." The closing movement is Solomon's slow turning (1 Kings 11): "But king Solomon loved many strange women" — a thousand small accommodations compounding across a lifetime until "his heart was not perfect with the Lord his God." David sinned greatly yet stayed whole; Solomon sinned subtly and came apart — and even the judgment is folded with mercy, "for David's sake," through which the Messianic promise would still come. Drawn from the full Gospel Library — scripture, General Conference (President Uchtdorf's "A Matter of a Few Degrees," President Nelson and President Eyring on the temple), the Old Testament Student Manual, Latter-day Saint scholarship, the Interpreter Foundation, and the Jewish historian Josephus.
item.itunes:summary: A 3h56m deep dive on 2 Samuel 11–12 and 1 Kings 3; 6–9; 11 around one question — is my heart whole with God? David falls by a chain of choices and murders Uriah; Nathan's "Thou art the man" draws the confession "I have sinned against the Lord," yet consequence remains; Solomon asks for "an understanding heart" and builds and dedicates the temple — the spine of the week — praying "hear thou in heaven… and when thou hearest, forgive," with God's promise "mine eyes and mine heart shall be there perpetually"; and the wisest man slowly lets his heart divide until "his heart was not perfect with the Lord his God." The standard: "Let your heart therefore be perfect with the Lord our God" (1 Kings 8:61). Drawn from the full Gospel Library plus Josephus.

item.title: CFM Week 25 — 1 Samuel 17–18; 24–26; 2 Samuel 5–7: The Battle Is the Lord's
item.description: A 4h09m doctrinal deep dive on 1 Samuel 17–18; 24–26 and 2 Samuel 5–7 — the rise of David, traced through five movements held together by one shepherd-boy's conviction: "the battle is the Lord's" (1 Samuel 17:47). The first movement is David and Goliath (1 Samuel 17): for forty days a giant defied "the armies of the living God," and Israel measured him against themselves and despaired — David measured him against God and found him small, refusing Saul's armor ("I have not proved them") and running toward the giant in the name of the Lord of Hosts, "that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel" — read with President Kimball's "The Davids and the Goliaths" (October 1974). The second is covenant friendship and envy (1 Samuel 18): the soul of Jonathan "knit with the soul of David," the crown prince stripping off robe and sword to yield his royal claim to the Lord's anointed — chesed, covenant love — set against Saul's curdling jealousy at "David his ten thousands." The third is vengeance left to the Lord (1 Samuel 24–26): twice David spares Saul ("the Lord forbid that I should… stretch forth mine hand against… the Lord's anointed"), and between them the wise Abigail intercepts David's wrath against the foolish Nabal, taking the offense upon herself and keeping him "from avenging myself with mine own hand" — Abigail read as a type of Christ the Mediator, with Sister Kristin M. Yee's "Beauty for Ashes" (April 2022). The fourth is king over Israel and the ark (2 Samuel 5–6): Zion taken and made "the city of David," David still "inquiring of the Lord" before battle, the sobering death of Uzzah who reached out to steady the ark (President David O. McKay on "steadying the ark," Conference Report, April 1936), and David dancing "before the Lord with all his might" while Michal despised him — reverence and exuberant gladness both right when offered the Lord's way. The closing movement is the Davidic covenant (2 Samuel 7): David would build God a house, and God instead promises to build David a house — "thy throne shall be established for ever" — the dualistic prophecy that is the seedbed of all messianic hope, fulfilled in Jesus Christ, the Son of David and Eternal King. Sources span the full Gospel Library — scripture, General Conference (President Kimball, Sister Yee, President McKay), the Old Testament Student Manual, Latter-day Saint scholarship, the Maxwell Institute, the Interpreter Foundation, the Journal of Discourses, and the Jewish historian Josephus.
item.itunes:summary: A 4h09m deep dive on 1 Samuel 17–18; 24–26 and 2 Samuel 5–7. Drawn from the full Gospel Library plus Josephus.

item.title: CFM Week 24 — 1 Samuel 8–10; 13; 15–16: The Lord Looketh on the Heart
item.description: A 3h57m doctrinal deep dive on 1 Samuel 8–10; 13; 15–16 — the story of two kings and one searching question: what is God actually looking for? Five extended sections. The first takes up Israel's demand for a king "like all the nations" (1 Samuel 8) and the Lord's piercing reply, "they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them" — read alongside Mosiah 29 and the warning of "the manner of the king" who will take and take. The second follows Saul, chosen and anointed (1 Samuel 9–10): a young man searching for lost donkeys who is led by providence to Samuel, given "another heart," filled with the Spirit, then found hiding "among the stuff" — a genuine humility that makes the later fall the more sobering. The third is the failure to wait (1 Samuel 13): under pressure, with his army scattering, Saul "forced himself" and offered the burnt offering — "thou hast done foolishly" — read with President Uchtdorf's "A Matter of a Few Degrees" on how small deviations compound. The fourth is the doctrinal keystone (1 Samuel 15): commanded to destroy Amalek utterly, Saul spares Agag and the best of the flocks and calls it sacrifice, drawing Samuel's immortal answer, "to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams… rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft," and Saul's confession, "I feared the people, and obeyed their voice." The closing section is the verse that names the whole lesson (1 Samuel 16): Samuel sent to Bethlehem, son after impressive son passing by, until the Lord chooses the shepherd boy David — "man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart" — the Spirit coming mightily upon David and departing from Saul. Sources span the full Gospel Library — scripture, General Conference (Elder Barcellos's 2025 "The Lord Looketh on the Heart," President Uchtdorf, Elder Hales, Elder Robbins), the Old Testament Student Manual, Latter-day Saint scholarship, the Interpreter Foundation, the Journal of Discourses, the Ante-Nicene Fathers, and the Jewish historian Josephus.
item.itunes:summary: A 3h57m deep dive on 1 Samuel 8–10; 13; 15–16. Israel demands a king "like all the nations" and so rejects the Lord as King; Saul is anointed and given "another heart," then unravels — he cannot wait (chapter 13, "thou hast done foolishly"), he obeys only partway and calls it sacrifice (chapter 15, "to obey is better than sacrifice"), and confesses "I feared the people." So the Lord turns to a shepherd boy in Bethlehem: "man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7). A good beginning lost through small deviations, partial obedience, and the fear of man — and the heart God actually weighs. Drawn from the full Gospel Library plus Josephus.

item.title: CFM Week 23 — Ruth; 1 Samuel 1–7: My Heart Rejoiceth in the Lord
item.description: A 4h20m doctrinal deep dive on Ruth and 1 Samuel 1–7 — two women brought from emptiness to fullness, and a boy who learned to say "Speak, Lord." Five extended sections. The first walks the road home with Ruth — the famine that drove a family from Bethlehem ("house of bread") into Moab, Naomi's losses, and the most beautiful vow of loyalty in the Old Testament ("thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God"), built on the Hebrew chesed, covenant love. The second meets the redeemer at the gate: Boaz the go'el, the kinsman-redeemer who "buys back" lost family and raises up its name — deliverance at a price he freely pays — placing Ruth, a Gentile convert, in the lineage of Jesus Christ (Matthew 1:5), and standing as a type of the Savior our Kinsman-Redeemer. The third is Hannah's prayer and song at Shiloh — the childless wife who "poured out her soul," misjudged by Eli as drunk, who lent her son Samuel back to the Lord and sang "My heart rejoiceth in the Lord" (1 Samuel 2:1–10), the forerunner of Mary's Magnificat — set against Eli's failure with his own corrupt sons. The fourth is the doctrinal keystone: the boy Samuel learning to recognize the Lord's voice in the night, "Speak, Lord; for thy servant heareth," in a day when "the word of the Lord was precious." The closing section follows the ark — Israel treating it as a good-luck charm and being routed, "Ichabod, the glory is departed," the ark humbling the Philistine god Dagon, and Samuel's call to repentance at Mizpah — ending with the stone Ebenezer, "Hitherto hath the Lord helped us." Sources span the full Gospel Library — scripture, General Conference, the Journal of Discourses, the Ante-Nicene Fathers, Latter-day Saint scholarship, the Interpreter Foundation, and the Jewish historian Josephus.
item.itunes:summary: A 4h20m deep dive on Ruth and 1 Samuel 1–7. Ruth's vow of covenant chesed and the road from "Mara" (bitter) back to fullness, Boaz the kinsman-redeemer (go'el) as a type of Christ who places Ruth in the lineage of Jesus, Hannah pouring out her soul and singing "My heart rejoiceth in the Lord" (forerunner of Mary's Magnificat), the boy Samuel learning "Speak, Lord; for thy servant heareth," and the ark, Ichabod, and Samuel's Ebenezer — "Hitherto hath the Lord helped us." Drawn from the full Gospel Library plus Josephus.

item.title: Doctrinal Deep Dive — From Grace to Grace: Doctrine and Covenants 93:11–20
item.description: A 4h22m doctrinal deep dive on Doctrine and Covenants 93:11–20 — the quiet, astonishing claim that even the Savior "received not of the fulness at the first, but received grace for grace," and "continued from grace to grace, until he received a fulness." Five extended sections. The first defines grace itself — the Greek charis, the Bible Dictionary's "divine means of help or strength," and the two faces of grace: redeeming grace that cleanses and forgives, and enabling grace that makes "weak things become strong" (Ether 12:27). The second traces Christ's own growth — "the child grew," "Jesus increased in wisdom and stature," and the teaching that the Son Himself grew from grace to grace. The third takes up the great misunderstanding — grace versus works — and resolves it through Ephesians 2 and James 2 and a careful reading of 2 Nephi 25:23 ("after all we can do"), with Stephen E. Robinson's parable of the bicycle and Brad Wilcox's piano-lesson analogy. The fourth follows where the pattern leads — being "glorified in me as I am in the Father" (D&C 93:20) — read alongside the earliest Christian writers (Irenaeus, Justin Martyr, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, and the post-Nicene capstone Athanasius) and the Prophet Joseph Smith's King Follett teaching of going "from grace to grace, from exaltation to exaltation." The closing section brings it home to daily discipleship: the sacrament as weekly grace for grace, repentance as growth rather than only guilt, and the promise that slow, incremental growth is the very pattern God designed. The rare phrase "grace for grace" appears in only four places in all scripture — John 1:16, D&C 93:12, D&C 93:20, and Helaman 12:24. Sources span the full Gospel Library — scripture, General Conference, BYU devotionals, Latter-day Saint scholarship, the Journal of Discourses, the Ante-Nicene Fathers, and the Interpreter Foundation.
item.itunes:summary: A 4h22m deep dive on D&C 93:11–20 — "from grace to grace." What grace is (redeeming and enabling), how even Christ "increased" and grew grace for grace, the grace-and-works question resolved through Ephesians 2, James 2, and 2 Nephi 25:23 ("after all we can do") with Robinson's bicycle parable and Wilcox's piano analogy, where the pattern leads — being "glorified… as I am in the Father" — read with the earliest Christian writers and Joseph Smith's King Follett sermon, and what it means for daily discipleship. Drawn from the full Gospel Library.

item.title: CFM Week 22 — Judges 2–4; 6–8; 13–16: The Cycle and the Deliverers
item.description: A 4h17m doctrinal deep dive on Judges 2–4; 6–8; 13–16 — the most honest book in the Old Testament about how people drift from God, and the most hopeful about how He keeps coming back for them. Five extended sections. The first lays down the cycle of Judges 2 — rest, forgetting, bondage, crying out, deliverance, relapse — the same wheel that turns through the Book of Mormon as the pride cycle. The second tells of Deborah, Barak, and Jael, with Sisera's nine hundred chariots of iron bogged down at the river Kishon and the reminder that "the Lord is gone out before thee." The third is the heart of the book: Gideon, the "least" of his family greeted as a "mighty man of valour," his altar Jehovah-shalom, the sign of the fleece, and an army shrunk from 32,000 to just 300 "lest Israel vaunt themselves," followed by his noble refusal of a crown. The fourth follows Samson — the Nazarite vow set on him before birth, his Spirit-given strength squandered compromise by compromise until "he wist not that the Lord was departed from him," and a death that brought a greater deliverance than his life. The closing section ties every flawed and partial deliverer to the perfect and final Deliverer, Jesus Christ — reading Gideon's fleece, Jael's victory, and Samson through the eyes of the earliest Christian writers — and grounds it all in the promise that the Lord makes "weak things become strong" (Ether 12:27). Sources span the full Gospel Library — General Conference, the Journal of Discourses, the Ante-Nicene Fathers (Irenaeus, Lactantius, Hippolytus, Tertullian), the Interpreter Foundation, Latter-day Saint scholarship, and the Jewish historian Josephus.
item.itunes:summary: A 4h17m deep dive on Judges 2–4; 6–8; 13–16. The cycle of Judges 2 (the same wheel as the Book of Mormon's pride cycle), Deborah and Jael against Sisera's iron chariots, Gideon's army cut to 300 "lest Israel vaunt themselves," Samson's Nazarite vow and the death that delivered more than his life, and the thread that ties every flawed deliverer to the perfect One — Jesus Christ — grounded in "weak things become strong" (Ether 12:27).

item.title: CFM Week 21 — Joshua 1–8; 23–24: Be Strong and of a Good Courage
item.description: A 4h37m doctrinal deep dive on Joshua 1–8; 23–24. Five extended sections trace the commission of Joshua (Yehoshua / Yeshua — the same name as Jesus) and the "I will not fail thee" promise rooted in Deuteronomy 31; Rahab the Canaanite whose scarlet cord becomes a Passover-and-cross type (Justin Martyr, Origen, Aphrahat) and lands her in the genealogy of Christ; the crossing of the Jordan and the fall of Jericho read as baptismal and conquest typology, with a five-layer treatment of the herem ("utter destruction") problem; Joshua's farewell covenant at Shechem in its ancient suzerain-vassal treaty form, with the binary "Choose you this day" call; and a closing section on living the covenant day to day. Sources span the full Gospel Library — General Conference, the Journal of Discourses, the Ante-Nicene Fathers, BYU Studies, the Maxwell Institute, and the Interpreter Foundation.
item.itunes:summary: A 4h37m doctrinal deep dive on Joshua 1–8; 23–24. The commission of Joshua, Rahab and the scarlet cord, the crossing of the Jordan and walls of Jericho as baptism-and-conquest typology, the herem problem, Joshua's covenant farewell at Shechem with "Choose you this day," and the Joshua/Jesus (Yehoshua/Yeshua) typology.

item.title: CFM Week 20 — Deuteronomy 6–8; 15; 18; 29–30; 34: Moses' Farewell on the Plains of Moab
item.description: A one-hour-forty-minute deep dive on Moses' farewell sermon. Seven sections trace the most theologically concentrated chapters in the Old Testament: the Shema (Deut 6), the great commandment to love God with all thy heart, the lesson of the manna (Deut 8) that Christ would quote in the wilderness, the year of release and debt forgiveness (Deut 15), the prophecy of a prophet like unto Moses (Deut 18) pointing forward to Christ and Joseph Smith, the sweeping blessings and cursings of the covenant (Deut 29–30), Moses' invitation to "choose life," and finally the death of Moses on Pisgah (Deut 34) — a death so unique that the Bible says no man knows the place of his burial, and Latter-day Saints have something more to say about that.
item.itunes:summary: A one-hour-forty-minute deep dive on Moses' farewell sermon. item.title: CFM Doctrinal Deep Dive — The Sons of Levi: Malachi 3 and the Restoration Priesthood
item.description: A two-and-a-half-hour doctrinal deep dive on Malachi 3:1-4 and the offering of the sons of Levi in righteousness. Who were the sons of Levi? Why does the Lord promise to purify them as gold and silver? Seven sections trace the Levitical priesthood from Sinai through the Restoration — covenant origins, Aaronic and Melchizedek orders, the Nauvoo Temple revelation (D&C 124), and the modern fulfillment of Malachi's prophecy through ordinances of the temple.

Six sections covering scripture, the Ante-Nicene Fathers, modern conference, the Restoration, and the Two Comforters doctrine.
